title: Instruction-Level Parallelism and Advanced Pipelining
subtitle: Doing more than one instruction per cycle, and what stops us.

references.title: The Processor
references.topics: Parallelism via instructions: multiple issue, static and dynamic multiple-issue processors

references.title: Advanced Pipelining and Instruction-Level Parallelism
references.topics: Concepts and challenges of ILP; multiple-issue processors; limits on ILP

objectives: Explain how a superscalar processor issues several instructions per cycle
Identify true, anti and output dependences and control dependences
Explain what limits ILP and why more issue width gives diminishing returns

steps.question: The pipeline of Class 12 finishes at best one instruction per cycle. How could a processor finish two, or four?
clues: Find instructions that **do not depend on each other**.
Build **more than one** execution path and start several instructions per cycle.
But real programs have **dependences** that limit how much overlap is possible.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Instruction-level parallelism

items: **ILP**: instructions in the same program that can be executed **at the same time** because they do not depend on each other
A pipeline already overlaps instructions, but at best 1 instruction **per cycle**
To go beyond, issue **several** instructions in the same cycle
**IPC** (instructions per cycle) = 1 / CPI

steps.why: Once the clock rate stopped rising (Class 2), designers looked for parallelism inside a single program.
steps.real: Phones and laptops execute several instructions in each clock cycle.

explainAgain.beginner: A single cook can only do one thing at a time; two cooks can chop and boil at the same time, but only if the tasks do not depend on each other.

steps.title: Independent vs dependent instructions

left.title: Independent (can overlap)
items: `add r1,r2,r3`
`sub r4,r5,r6`
`mul r7,r8,r9`
No instruction uses a result of another

right.title: Dependent (must wait)
items: `add r1,r2,r3`
`add r4,r1,r5`
`add r6,r4,r7`
Each one needs the previous result

steps.why: Independent instructions are the raw material of ILP; a chain of dependences has none.
steps.real: Compilers and hardware search for independent instructions all the time.

steps.title: Try it: independent instructions

blocks.title: Six independent instructions (mul takes 3 cycles)
blocks.hint: Change **Instructions issued per cycle** from 1 to 2 to 4 and compare the cycles and the IPC.

steps.why: With 1 per cycle: 8 cycles (IPC 0.75). With 2: 6 cycles (IPC 1.0). With 4: 5 cycles (IPC 1.2).

steps.question: The six independent instructions run in 6 cycles on a 2-wide machine. What is the IPC?

reveal.text: IPC = 6 instructions ÷ 6 cycles = **1.0**. The machine could in theory do 2 per cycle, but the first cycles are spent filling the pipeline.

steps.result: Real IPC is always below the peak (the issue width).

steps.title: Calculate: IPC and CPI
steps.why: The width-4 run above gave 6 instructions in 5 cycles: IPC 1.2, only 30% of the peak of 4.

steps.question: What is IPC?
steps.why: IPC = instructions divided by cycles; it is the inverse of CPI.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.b: Instructions that can run at the same time

steps.why: These four terms recur in every later class.

steps.title: Issuing several instructions per cycle

items: A **superscalar** processor starts **more than one instruction per cycle**
The **issue width** is the maximum number started together (2-wide, 4-wide, ...)
It needs duplicated hardware: several ALUs, more register ports, more cache ports
Extra logic checks which instructions in the window are independent

steps.why: More width raises the ceiling, but the real speed depends on how much independent work the program contains.
steps.real: Typical laptop cores issue 4 to 8 instructions per cycle at peak.

mistake.right: The peak is 4 times higher; real programs have dependences and reach far less.

explainAgain.beginner: A four-lane road is useless if the cars in front of you are all queuing for the same exit.

steps.title: Try it: a dependence chain

blocks.title: Four dependent adds
blocks.hint: Change the issue width: does anything improve?

steps.why: Every add needs the result of the one before: widths 1, 2 and 4 all take 9 cycles.

steps.question: How many cycles do the four dependent adds take on a 4-wide machine?

reveal.text: The chain forces the instructions to run one after the other, so the extra width does not help: **9 cycles**, the same as width 1.

steps.result: ILP is a property of the program as well as the machine.

steps.title: Diminishing returns
steps.why: Going from 1 to 2 saved 2 cycles; going from 2 to 4 saved only 1. Each extra unit of width adds less.
steps.real: This is why designers do not build 32-wide cores: the hardware cost and power grow faster than the speed.

steps.statement: A wider superscalar processor always runs a program proportionally faster.
steps.why: The speed-up is limited by the dependences in the program.

steps.question: Which resource does a 4-wide superscalar need more of?
steps.why: Several instructions are started at once, so several units and ports are needed.
feedback: Width has a real hardware and power cost.

steps.title: Who finds the parallelism?

head: Static (compile time)
Dynamic (run time)
rows: The hardware reorders instructions as they run
The actual run-time values and delays

steps.why: Both aim at the same thing: put independent instructions close together so they can overlap.
steps.real: Embedded processors lean on the compiler; high-end laptop and server cores rely on dynamic hardware too.

steps.title: Static scheduling: reorder to hide a delay

left.title: Original (loads stall their users)
items: `add r2,r1,r3`
`sub r5,r4,r6`

right.title: Scheduled by the compiler
items: `add r2,r1,r3`
`sub r5,r4,r6`

steps.why: Starting both loads first hides each load's delay behind the other: the same result in fewer cycles.
steps.real: Compilers do this routinely when they target a pipelined or superscalar machine.

steps.title: Run the reordering
steps.why: Same four instructions, same results: 10 cycles become 7 on a scalar machine and 9 become 6 on a 2-wide one.

steps.title: Loop unrolling

blocks.text: A loop body of load, add, store has little ILP. **Unrolling** copies the body several times so the compiler can **interleave** independent iterations.

blocks.code:
for (i = 0; i < 4; i++)
    b[i] = a[i] + c;      // each iteration is independent

head: Version (in-order machine)
Width 1
Width 2
Width 4
rows: Unrolled 4× and interleaved by the compiler

steps.why: Unrolling by itself helps little: the instructions must also be scheduled so that independent ones sit side by side.
steps.real: Optimizing compilers unroll hot loops and schedule them; the result is much faster on wide processors.

mistake.wrong: Unrolling alone makes the loop faster.
mistake.right: The gain comes from the interleaving it enables.

steps.title: Run the unrolled loop
steps.why: Compare the two schedules at width 4: 23 cycles against 8.

steps.question: After the compiler interleaves the unrolled loop, how many cycles does it need on a 2-wide in-order machine?

reveal.text: Interleaved: **9 cycles** at width 2 (14 at width 1, 8 at width 4). The original order took 23.

steps.result: Notice how little a wide machine helps until the code is rescheduled.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why might a processor designer prefer dynamic scheduling even though it is more complex?
steps.answer: Dynamic scheduling works on the code as it runs, so it adapts to delays the compiler cannot know (such as a cache miss) and it speeds up old binaries without recompiling. The cost is complex hardware and extra power. Static scheduling is simple but cannot react to run-time events.

questions.a: The compiler, before the program runs.
It exposes independent iterations that can be interleaved.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of dynamic scheduling?
questions.a: It adapts to run-time delays and works with old code.

steps.title: Kinds of dependences

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: A later instruction needs the value an earlier one produces (RAW)
A later instruction writes a register an earlier one reads (WAR)
Two instructions write the same register (WAW)
An instruction's execution depends on a branch

steps.why: True dependences are real limits. Name dependences are only about reusing a register name and can often be removed by renaming (Class 15). Control dependences are limited by branch prediction (Class 16).
steps.real: Compilers analyse these dependences to decide which instructions may be reordered.

mistake.right: Only true dependences are fundamental; name dependences can be removed by renaming.

deeper.text: Dependences through memory (a store followed by a load of the same address) are also true dependences.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: Three instructions: 1) add r1,r2,r3  2) sub r4,r1,r5  3) mul r1,r6,r7. Which statement is wrong?
lines: 1. Instruction 2 has a true dependence on instruction 1 (RAW on r1).
2. Instruction 3 has an anti-dependence with instruction 2 (WAR on r1).
3. Instruction 3 has an output dependence with instruction 1 (WAW on r1).
4. Instruction 3 has a true dependence on instruction 1.
steps.explain: Instruction 3 writes r1 but does not read the r1 of instruction 1: that is only an output (name) dependence.

steps.title: What limits ILP?

items: **True data dependences**: the chain of results cannot be shortened
**Control dependences**: about one instruction in five is a branch, so the processor can look only a few instructions ahead before a branch
**A finite window**: hardware can examine only a limited number of instructions
**A finite number of registers and execution units**
**Memory latency**: a cache miss stalls everything that depends on the load
**Cost and power**: wider machines cost more silicon and energy for less gain

steps.why: Studies on real programs find that ILP often stays below about 2 to 4 for realistic hardware, even though code in some loops has far more.
steps.real: This is the reason industry turned to multiple cores (Class 23).

explainAgain.beginner: Even with unlimited cooks, a recipe whose steps all depend on the previous one can only go step by step.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Why did processor designers move from ever-wider cores to many cores?
ideas: ILP in a single program is limited by dependences and branches.
Wider issue and bigger windows cost power and area for diminishing gains.
Several threads supply independent work for several cores (thread-level parallelism).
The programmer must then expose the parallelism (Class 23).

steps.question: Which dependence is a fundamental limit that renaming cannot remove?
steps.why: A value that must be computed before it is used cannot be avoided.

steps.question: Define ILP in one sentence.
steps.answer: The amount of independent instructions in a program that can execute at the same time.
steps.solution: Instructions with no dependence on each other can overlap.

steps.question: Six independent instructions run in 5 cycles. What are the IPC and the CPI?
Four dependent adds run on a 4-wide machine. How many cycles, and why is the width not useful?
steps.answer: 9 cycles; each add needs the previous result, so they cannot overlap.
steps.solution: Dependent instructions run in sequence regardless of the issue width.
steps.hint: Look at the chain of results.

steps.question: For 1) add r1,r2,r3 2) sub r4,r1,r5 3) mul r1,r6,r7 name each dependence (RAW, WAR or WAW) and the instructions involved.
steps.answer: 1→2 RAW on r1; 2→3 WAR on r1; 1→3 WAW on r1.
steps.solution: Instruction 2 reads the r1 written by 1 (RAW). Instruction 3 writes r1 after 2 reads it (WAR) and after 1 wrote it (WAW).
steps.title: Exam practice: dependences

steps.question: lw r1,0(r10); add r2,r1,r3; lw r4,4(r10); sub r5,r4,r6 (loads take 2 cycles). Reorder to improve the in-order 2-wide schedule and give the cycles before and after.
steps.answer: Reorder to lw r1; lw r4; add r2; sub r5. Before: 9 cycles. After: 6 cycles.
steps.solution: Starting both loads first lets the load delays overlap, and each add/sub then finds its operand ready.
steps.mistake: Moving an add before the load it uses.
steps.title: Exam practice: scheduling

steps.question: The six independent instructions take 8, 6 and 5 cycles at widths 1, 2 and 4. Give the IPC for each and say why going from width 2 to 4 helps less than from 1 to 2.
steps.answer: IPC 0.75, 1.0 and 1.2. Width 1→2 saves 2 cycles, 2→4 only saves 1.
steps.solution: The pipeline fill and the mul's 3-cycle latency are fixed costs; once most of the independent work overlaps, extra width has little left to overlap.
steps.mistake: Believing IPC equals the issue width.
steps.title: Exam practice: calculation

steps.question: Explain why true dependences limit ILP but name dependences (WAR, WAW) usually do not.
steps.answer: A true dependence is an actual flow of a value, so the consumer must wait for the producer. A name dependence only arises because two instructions reuse the same register name; giving them different registers (renaming) removes it without changing the result, so it need not limit parallelism.
steps.solution: A strong answer states that renaming removes name dependences.
steps.mistake: Saying name dependences are impossible to remove.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: ILP is the parallelism between independent instructions of one program.
IPC = instructions ÷ cycles; CPI is its inverse.
A superscalar issues several instructions per cycle (the issue width), but the real IPC is far below the peak.
A chain of true dependences cannot run in parallel whatever the width.
Static scheduling: the compiler reorders and unrolls loops. Dynamic scheduling: the hardware reorders at run time.
Dependences: true (RAW), anti (WAR), output (WAW), and control; ILP is limited by data, branches, window size and cost.

mistakes.right: Its peak is 4 times higher; dependences limit the real gain.

mistakes.wrong: Unrolling alone speeds up a loop.
mistakes.right: The compiler must also interleave the independent iterations.
Name dependences can be removed by renaming; true dependences cannot.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Instruction-level parallelism lets a processor start several independent instructions in the same cycle. Superscalar designs have several execution units, but the achieved IPC depends on dependences in the program, branches, window size and hardware cost. The compiler (static scheduling) or the hardware (dynamic scheduling) tries to bring independent instructions together; true dependences remain a hard limit.

questions.question: What does ILP stand for?
questions.misconception: It is parallelism among instructions of one program.

questions.statement: A superscalar processor can start more than one instruction per cycle.
questions.misconception: The issue width states how many.

questions.question: Six independent instructions on a 2-wide in-order machine take:

questions.why: The dependence chain removes any gain from width.
questions.misconception: Each add waits for the previous result.

questions.question: Who performs static scheduling?
questions.why: Static means decided at compile time.
questions.misconception: Dynamic scheduling is done by the hardware.

questions.question: The original lw/add/lw/sub sequence takes 10 cycles on a 1-wide machine. After the compiler moves the second load up, it takes:
questions.why: Two overlapping loads remove most of the delay: 7 cycles.
questions.misconception: Ideal for 4 instructions with 2-cycle loads is more than 4.

questions.question: add r1,r2,r3 followed later by mul r1,r6,r7 is which dependence?
questions.why: Both write r1: an output dependence.
questions.misconception: No value flows from one to the other.

questions.question: The loop unrolled 4× and interleaved by the compiler takes how many cycles on a 4-wide in-order machine (the naive order takes 23)?
questions.why: Interleaving brings it to 8 cycles at width 4.

items.a: Independent instructions that can execute at the same time.
One that issues several instructions per cycle.

items.q: Why does more width give diminishing returns?
items.a: Dependences and fixed delays limit the overlap available.
